title: What Harvard & Stanford did *NOT* teach us
summary: In the Season 3 finale the sisters do roses and thorns (Cherie's 30-day workout streak and heavier late-20s dating conversations; Jean's friends leaving LA and her positive return to dating after 8+ years) and then distill the season's guest lessons: Vu Tran's 'go max dumb' first-principles approach, Imran Khan's emotional self-regulation, the fact that both Imran and Jeremy Liew were fired early and still built huge careers, and Jonah Goodheart's permission to pause. They preview a Season 4 shift toward topic-based, sister-to-sister explainer episodes.

ideas.idea: A streak-based goal like being active 30 days in a row works even when you keep resetting the clock, because the goal itself keeps you showing up.
ideas.detail: Cherie has made it 10 days then 14 days before a skipped day reset her count, yet she is in her best physical shape in years and sees visible abs for the first time, which she calls a lagging indicator of consistency since January.

ideas.idea: Dating in your late 20s approaching 30 is a life transition: conversations move from fun to compatibility, engagement and who wakes up with the baby, requiring more vulnerability and carrying higher stakes.
ideas.detail: Cherie says she hasn't had these conversations before and finds them harder and messier, while Jean, newly single after a long engagement, is enjoying the lighter 'ha ha hee hee' phase.

ideas.idea: Returning to dating after 8+ years can be as fun as before; a positive first experience matters because a string of bad dates delivers little cuts that crush the spirit.
ideas.detail: Jean worried it would be a totally new paradigm being almost 10 years older, and the unknown felt more vast than ever, but it has been encouraging so far.

ideas.idea: 'Go max dumb' to succeed: drop to first principles, ask why repeatedly, and admit when you don't understand, because trying to seem a little smart leaves you a 'midwit'.
ideas.detail: From the Season 3 episode with Vu Tran, which resonated most with subscribers. The hosts add that intellectually honest people who say 'we can't move forward until I understand this' earn more respect than those who pretend.

ideas.idea: The smartest people are the least afraid to say they don't know, and they acknowledge there's always more to learn even when they're billionaire investors.
ideas.detail: Jeremy Liew prefaced his hot take on nationalizing AI investment with 'I have a lot more research to do' and called it a strong opinion weakly held, which the hosts tie to the 'max dumb' concept.

ideas.idea: Fear of looking dumb in front of peers holds you back in class, business school and the workplace; if you don't speak up you only hurt yourself, and others usually share your question.
ideas.detail: Studying computer science at Columbia in male-dominated, cutthroat classes, Cherie wouldn't raise her hand despite professors being kind one-on-one; this became her 'villain origin story' as president of Columbia Women in Computer Science, building a psychologically safe community with conferences and networking events.

ideas.idea: Emotional self-regulation, never getting too excited or too depressed, is a source of power for long-term success because failures don't drag you down.
ideas.detail: Imran Khan attributes this trait to his success riding roller coasters as an investor on massive deals and as Snapchat's chief strategy officer through the IPO.

ideas.idea: Being fired for performance early on is a blip in a long career: both Imran Khan and Jeremy Liew were fired, learned from it, and their next big opportunity was born from that moment.
ideas.detail: Neither firing appears on their LinkedIn or in any Forbes or Time profile; the world would never have known had the hosts not asked about failures. Jean cautions it's not a guarantee everyone bounces back, but a bad moment doesn't have to define you.

ideas.idea: It is OK to pause: slowing down to care for your mental and physical health helps you get further, or 'slow down to speed up'.
ideas.detail: Advice from Jonah Goodheart, which felt like permission from a very successful person against the media image of founders always grinding. David Shim applies the same idea to public speaking by stepping away from a speech so it processes in the background.

ideas.idea: The sleep-under-your-desk founder archetype is not the only or right path; you also don't have to be a tech entrepreneur to be a startup founder.
ideas.detail: Jean absorbed the Silicon Valley 'founder is everything' mindset from very successful friends who slept in the office, and now sees it as context-dependent rather than required. Cherie admits she moves a mile a minute and doesn't give herself enough time to let things marinate.

ideas.idea: Season 4 will shift from guest interviews toward topic-based sister-to-sister explainers on networking, public speaking and business school, with more personalized interview questions.
ideas.detail: The hosts say Season 3's interview experiment worked, and the lesson learned is to be more nimble and personalized in interview questions going forward.
